“#Prevent, #Engage and#Act”

These were the three keywords I brought back home from the ReAct Asia Pacific Regional Conference on#AMR 2026, held in Jakarta last week.
 
Just ahead of#WAAW2026, clinicians, researchers, policymakers, CSOs and youth came together for two days to deliberate on a collective course of action for the years ahead.

#Prevent: The updated WHO Global Action Plan (2026–2036) puts prevention first. As one speaker put it, infection control, immunisation and WASH are among the most powerful AMR programmes we have. That means stopping infections before they need #antibiotics. Another session suggested teaching infection prevention to students early, so they carry it into practice and pass it on to their peers.

#Engage: AMR can’t be fixed by the health sector alone. One participant asked where the ministers of agriculture and environment were in the room, and another said the finance minister should be involved from day zero. The session that stayed with me most put people at the centre. AMR survivor Ankita Mitra reminded us that an infection may be diagnosed in one person, but the consequences are lived by an entire family. Civil society, communities, and young people have to be part of the solution.

#Act: Plans are only as good as their delivery. Most plans are not costed, and WHO shared that only about 10% of countries had domestic funding for their national action plans in 2024. The call from the room was to cost the plan, set measurable indicators, close the reporting gap, and scale what already works.

My biggest learning was seemingly obvious: AMR cannot be tackled without addressing the systemic challenges that sit beneath it. Plans stay unfunded, sectors stay siloed, and accountability stays weak. Access to antibiotics and diagnostics remains unequal, and infection control and primary care are still stretched thin. Climate change, disasters and conflict make all of this worse, because every flood or crisis can become an AMR event.
 
Underneath all of it is social inequity. Those who are poorer, more displaced, and further from care are the ones who face the weakest infection control, the limited access to diagnostics, and the highest costs when treatment fails. That is why so many well-designed plans don’t deliver: they work best for those who already have access. AMR is not only a health problem. It is a development problem and a health-system problem, and it needs to be treated as both.

We enountered some of these stories through the #SochSamajhKe fellowship, whichSuperheroes Against Superbugs organized earlier this year in collabortion withYouth Ki Awaaz. Seeing them echoed in Jakarta was a strong motivation for us to continue our work at SaS.

Sarsha Braim read her job offer on a bathroom break, halfway through a waitressing shift. Last month, she was in Cannes for MIPCOM (her first time in France), selling sport content to TV broadcasters alongside studios like Paramount and Disney.

Not long before that offer, she'd finished uni, applied for a few jobs in sport and heard nothing back. She had about 10 LinkedIn connections, all from one uni class, and was convinced that "I'm not some big CEO, so no one wants to hear from me."

55 days after joining TheSportsGrad Method, she was approached for a job at Inverleigh, a sports media company she'd never heard of.

So what did she do differently?

She started posting about ice hockey, a sport she genuinely loves and that hardly anyone in Australia was writing about. Then every time someone liked or reacted to a post, she sent them a connection request within 24 hours, "while it's still fresh," so they'd remember her name.

One of those people was a co-founder of Inverleigh. He passed her name on to the company's commercial director, and the director messaged her about a job.

Posting on LinkedIn gets you seen, but the job comes from what you do after someone notices you. Think of a like as a wave from across the street: you can wave back and keep walking, or you can cross the road and say hello.

Today Sarsha is Commercial Partnerships Manager, Asia Pacific, flying to Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia to sell sport content to broadcasters.

If you want to try it this week:

1. Pick a sport you could post about for months (bonus points if hardly anyone else is covering it)

2. Post one thing you've noticed about it through the lens of the job you want. Partnerships? Break down a club's sponsors. Events? Review a match day. Analytics? Unpack one stat

3. Set a 24-hour rule: everyone who reacts gets a connection request with a short note about the post

Devo, I know, most of your posts will get a handful of likes and plenty of people won't accept. 

But you're not waiting on a job ad anymore, and you only need the right person to remember you.

Big congrats to Sarsha, who has made her dream in sport come true. If you want to hear her full story, catch it on episode #378 of The SportsGrad Podcast withNathan Perrone.

My CV was rejected by a perfume brand. Not even invited for an interview, but it's ok :)

I have handled a local perfume brand before—from low awareness to shelf, from trial to repeat. And I have an obsession to build my own perfume brand. So I know the pain from the inside. 

What was in my head at that moment was this: "We need someone who can sell perfume in this crowded market".
My answer: "Everyone can sell perfume. Almost no one can make people REMEMBER perfume."

Look at their campaigns now: 15% - 35%++ discount in every campaign, and still low/not growing.

Discounts are not a strategy. It's a symptom.
A symptom that people try you once, and forget you tomorrow.

This is not a motivational post. This is my playbook.
👇 Day 10: #Perfume is Booming. But Everyone is#SellingPerfume.

THE DATA:
IDR 10,884 BILLION — Indonesia fragrance market 2025, 8.4% CAGR
USD 361M → USD 635M by 2035
9 out of 10 best-sellers on marketplace are LOCAL brands

Market is HUGE. Competition is BRUTAL.

WHY MOST BRANDS FAIL:
10 variants that all smell similar.
"Long-lasting 12 hours" + bottle photo + discount.
No hero. No story. No trial.
Result: Price war. No memory. No loyalty.

MY STRONG STRATEGY TO WIN:
1. SELL IDENTITY, NOT NOTES
Notes "vanilla, musk, amber."
But "For women who want to be remembered when they leave the room."

2. ONE HERO, NOT 10 COUSINS
1 HERO = 70% of budget, owns 1 persona
1 FIGHTER = for trial
1 LIMITED = for hype

Discovery Set 5 x 2ml + Full-Size Voucher.
Blind test on TikTok Live. Spray cards up to 500 micro-KOCs.
My KPI: 30% Discovery → Full Size in 14 days.
If not hit, your story is wrong, not your ad.

4. OWN TROPICAL + HALAL + LAYERING
Buyer asks in 5 seconds: Is it Halal? Will it last in Jakarta heat? Can I layer it?
Show 8-hour wear test + Halal cert upfront. Trust > Hype.

5. PROTECT YOUR HERO PRICE
Discovery Set = Entry. 30ml = Gift. 50ml = HERO, margin driver. 100ml = Premium.
Never discount the Hero. Discount the entry.

6. DIFFERENT JOBS PER CHANNEL, SAME PRICE
Marketplace & TikTok Shop = Trial
Beauty Store & Retail Store = Trust, Tester, Experience
Website = Loyalty, Refill, Member-Only

7. DROP, DON'T LAUNCH
500 pcs limited, numbered, early access.
Then let UGC sell: Scent Personality Quiz, Spray & React, and Rate My Perfume.

MY FORMULA:
Perfume = Trust x Memory x Trial

No Memory = Forgotten
No Trial = No Trust
No Trust = No Repeat

On 27 May 2003, Matt Mullenweg released the first version of WordPress. It started small: the blogging tool b2/cafelog was GPL licensed and its development had stalled, so in January 2003 Matt wrote on his blog that he wanted to fork it. Mike Little was the first to comment that he'd like to help, and together they shipped WordPress 0.70 for free.

Why it still matters to me: because b2's code was open, the old work wasn't lost, it could be picked up and carried on. Then in version 1.2 (May 2004) WordPress added a plugin architecture, so people could add features without touching the core. To this day a huge number of business websites, including many here in Indonesia, run on WordPress.

The lesson for me: a stalled project isn't always the end, and software that leaves room for others to extend it often outlives its first authors. If your developer walked away tomorrow, could someone else keep your app going?

Google Will Launch Android App Verification Requirement Globally In January 2027: 

An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Google announced Android developer verification last year, and despite numerous objections from developers and users, the company is forging ahead. It began blocking the installation of unregistered apps in some countries this fall, and the system is expanding globally soon. Google says it will start rolling out the requirement in all regions in January 2027, and it urges devs who still haven't registered their apps to do so soon.

The apps you download from the Play Store all come from verified developers, and Google's new requirement expands that requirement to apps from third-party sources. Once developer verification is live in your region, you won't be able to sideload apps unless the developer has registered with Google, which is framed as a security measure. Verification requires providing government identification and paying a $25 fee, which will allegedly make it harder for nefarious actors to distribute malware and scammy apps.

In September, Google launched verification in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand. Apparently, nothing exploded, so the company is now ready to expand. It previously said verification would go global in 2027, and it's not wasting any time with the January start. It says that verification will reach all devices within "several months." So far, Google is getting what it wanted from this initiative, with "millions" of non-Play apps already registered. The company says this accounts for more than 99 percent of global Android app installs.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

Key Signal to Watch

Indonesia faces a margin and inflation squeeze as 6–7% minimum wage hikes, BI tightening, and rising import costs collide with sub-5% consumer credit growth and fintech defaults above 5%. Labor-intensive manufacturers may curb formal hiring or pass costs onto prices, fueling core inflation. Key triggers to monitor include provincial UMP decisions (Nov 21), district UMK rates (Nov 25), and core CPI (Dec 1).

Anthropic just had a record-breaking IPO:
 
- Raised $81.3 billion, the largest initial raise of any IPO in history
- $2 trillion at the open. That’s bigger than the economy of every country except 15 (Turkey, Indonesia, the Netherlands and Switzerland are all smaller than Anthropic)
- A big first-day jump: it opened at $111.50 per share on the Nasdaq, 34.3% above the $83 offering price
- At the open, Anthropic was worth 12× Boeing, 16× Starbucks and nearly 8× Netflix
It opened 25% above Meta’s valuation
 
At the same time, here’s the employee side:
- 34 million Americans are knowledge workers, about 22% of all Americans employed
- Knowledge-worker payrolls have shrunk for 31 months in a row
- College grads now make up 1 in 3 of the long-term unemployed, up from 1 in 5 a decade ago
- 46% of professionals plan to look for a new job in the next six months, up from 27% a year ago. That’s roughly 15 million people
- There are only about 1.3 million openings in professional and business services. That’s about 12 people wanting to move for every open role
- Tech has been hit hardest: 172,000 announced US job cuts this year, more than any other industry, and up 21%
- Software postings are still 27.5% below 2020 levels, but nearly half of them now ask for AI skills
- Postings requiring AI skills grew 144% in a year
- OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind together have about 1,700 open roles. That’s about 9,000 people wanting to move for every frontier-lab job
 
The gap: we’ve built a $2 trillion company in six years, yet 15 million knowledge workers can’t find a clear path to their next role. Plenty of people want to move and plenty of jobs ask for AI skills. What’s missing is a trusted way to show who actually has them.
 
Takeaway:

Innovation is essential. It’s how we move forward, and slowing it down isn’t the answer. What matters now is filling the jobs that already exist faster, and today we’re not.
 
It still takes employers more than 2 months to fill a role, even though they now get nearly 3× as many applications per hire as in 2021. On the other side, the average job seeker spends 27 weeks out of work, longer than unemployment benefits last.
 
More applications, but no faster hiring.
 
We’ve taken the human out of hiring. Only 1 in 10 job seekers believes a person reviews their applications. We’re judging people by a static résumé that AI has polished, when what we need to understand is:
 - What people actually bring to the table, not just where they’ve worked
 - What they want to do next, not just what they’ve done
 - Who will actually succeed in a given role, which is deeply human: the expectations, the team, the culture
 
I’m optimistic that AI will eventually create more opportunities than it takes away. But we need to fill those opportunities faster, AND in a human way.

India's top 5 IT companies cut 6,981 jobs in FY26.
In the same year, the Indian IT industry added 1.4 lakh people.

So is AI taking IT jobs, or just changing who gets them?
I put this question to two founders who are building the AI themselves: Arpan Shukla andAkshat Mittal, co-founders of Techladder.AI, the team behind the voice AI platform Vaarti.

Arpan Shukla has led product atPaytm, Navi and GoTo Financial, Inc.l in Jakarta. Akshat Mittal started as a coder in 2013 and later droveVLCC's digital transformation as CPO. Today they run a bootstrapped, 18-member team in Gurugram where every single person codes.

What they told me on Sunbird Talks:
🔹 Will AI replace software engineers?
Jobs that only repeat work will go. The golden era of Indian IT is not over, it is shifting from supporting other people's products to building products India sells to the world.

🔹 Who is most at risk?
Not freshers, not leaders. Anyone who stopped upskilling. Many freshers can build a voice agent with vibe coding but can't explain one line of the code.

🔹 What does upskilling actually mean?
Not a Harvard certificate. If AI writes your code, take ownership of QA and release too. Learn prompting, not just tools.

🔹 Why is voice still the strongest sales channel?
Email, SMS and WhatsApp keep growing, but people still want to talk. AI voice agents are replacing the "press 1, press 2" IVR.

🔹 How much does an AI calling agent cost in India?
From ₹6 down to ₹3 per minute, billed on a 30-second pulse, versus ₹20,000 to ₹40,000 a month for one caller in a Tier 2/3 call centre.

🔹 Can a startup beat the big CRMs that launched their own voice bots?
"Everyone owns an oven. Not everyone can bake like a bakery."

🔹 Are AI calls safe and legal?
Their rules: KYC before any calling, consented data only, zero cold calling, and the agent always tells you it is an AI assistant.

The line from Vijay Shekhar Sharma's office wall that Arpan Shukla still lives by: Go big or go home.

Apache Struts 7.4.0: The Breaking Changes Developers Need to Check

Apache Struts 7.4.0 became generally available on October 2, 2026, alongside Struts 6.12.0, but the 7.4 release is not just a routine maintenance update for Java web applications. Its version notes contain a source-breaking change around SecurityMemberAccess, several deprecations, and a new HTML5 validation feature that can affect how older applications are configured. The 6.x line receives a separate release with a different compatibility profile, giving teams another path if moving to Struts 7 would require a larger Java and Jakarta EE migration.

Apache Struts 7.4.0 removes five SecurityMemberAccess setters

The most significant code-level change in Struts 7.4.0 is the removal of five development-mode configuration setters from SecurityMemberAccess. These include setters controlling development mode and several excluded-class and excluded-package settings, while the corresponding struts.devMode.* configuration properties themselves remain unchanged. Applications that directly call those Java setters can therefore encounter source-level failures even though an application's existing configuration properties may still look familiar. Apache's own release notes classify this as a breaking change, so it deserves a compile-and-test pass rather than being treated as an invisible patch update.
